Carbon parity after invasive plant removal, and the crediting gap it exposes

A parity synthesis across seven invaded systems, and an audit of six carbon standards that cannot reward the result

# Rendering this manuscript runs the entire analysis. Every number in the text, every
# table and every figure below is produced by the R code in this document, so the prose
# and the results cannot drift apart. Nothing is fetched over the network: both inputs
# are parameter tables held in 02.inputs, each row carrying the source it was read from.
# Base R only, no packages beyond knitr, so the document renders on any R installation.

library(knitr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)

repo <- normalizePath("..")
IN   <- file.path(repo, "02.inputs")
TBL  <- file.path(repo, "03.outputs", "tables")
FIG  <- file.path(repo, "03.outputs", "figures")
dir.create(TBL, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(FIG, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(20260730)          # the Monte Carlo below is reproducible from this seed
NSIM      <- 10000          # draws per system
HORIZON   <- 300            # years; parity is reported as not reached beyond this
CREDIT    <- 40             # years; the AFOLU crediting period used for the crediting test
DEMINIMIS <- 0.05           # the 5 percent de minimis threshold used by Verra
DEFAULT_CV <- 0.20          # dispersion assumed where a source reports none
CO2_C     <- 44 / 12        # conversion from carbon to carbon dioxide equivalent

# formatting helpers used throughout
f1  <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2  <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f0  <- function(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
pc  <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
yr  <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "not reached", sprintf("%.0f", x))
# The parameter table is long format, one row per parameter per system, so provenance
# travels with the value. Tier A is measured with dispersion, B measured as a point
# estimate, C derived by arithmetic shown in this document, D transferred from another
# system or a global default because nothing system specific exists.
par_long <- read.csv(file.path(IN, "carbon-parameters.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sysmeta  <- read.csv(file.path(IN, "systems.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# any parameter still flagged provisional is a hard stop: the manuscript must not report
# a number that has not been read from a source
prov <- par_long[par_long$tier == "P", ]
if (nrow(prov) > 0) {
  stop("Provisional parameters remain in carbon-parameters.csv: ",
       paste(unique(paste(prov$system_id, prov$parameter)), collapse = ", "))
}

# pull a single parameter for a single system
getp <- function(sid, p, field = "value") {
  r <- par_long[par_long$system_id == sid & par_long$parameter == p, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  as.numeric(r[[field]][1])
}
gett <- function(sid, p) {
  r <- par_long[par_long$system_id == sid & par_long$parameter == p, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(NA_character_)
  r$tier[1]
}

SYS <- sysmeta$system_id
names(SYS) <- sysmeta$system_short

# Evidence class is derived from the parameter tiers rather than asserted in the input file,
# so the manuscript cannot describe a system as quantified unless the parameters say so. A
# system is quantified only where both stocks and the invader's own aboveground carbon are
# measured or derived rather than transferred from elsewhere.
KEYPAR <- c("C_inv", "C_nat", "AGB_inv")
sysmeta$evidence_class <- sapply(sysmeta$system_id, function(s)
  if (all(sapply(KEYPAR, function(p) gett(s, p)) %in% c("A", "B", "C")))
    "Quantified" else "Indicative")
n_quant <- sum(sysmeta$evidence_class == "Quantified")
n_indic <- sum(sysmeta$evidence_class == "Indicative")
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The two trajectory parity model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Both scenarios are monomolecular approaches to an asymptote, the standard form for
# stock recovery toward a carrying capacity. C(t) = K - (K - C0) exp(-r t).
#
# LEAVE: the invader is retained. The stock relaxes from the measured invaded stock
# C_inv toward the invaded asymptote K_inv at rate r_inv. Where the invaded state is
# already at equilibrium, K_inv equals C_inv and the trajectory is flat.
#
# REMOVE: at t = 0 the stock falls instantaneously by the removal debt D, then relaxes
# from that reduced starting point toward the native reference stock C_nat at rate
# r_nat, the rate at which native vegetation reaccumulates carbon on cleared ground.

approach <- function(t, C0, K, r) K - (K - C0) * exp(-r * t)

C_leave  <- function(t, C_inv, K_inv, r_inv) approach(t, C_inv, K_inv, r_inv)

# The debt is the carbon the removal puts into the atmosphere, or removes from the site
# without replacing: the released fraction of the invader's own aboveground stock, plus
# any soil carbon lost to the disturbance, plus the operational emissions of clearing.
debt <- function(AGB_inv, f_rel, dSOC, E_op) AGB_inv * f_rel + dSOC + E_op

C_remove <- function(t, C_inv, D, C_nat, r_nat) approach(t, C_inv - D, C_nat, r_nat)

# Carbon parity is the first time the removal trajectory catches the leave trajectory.
# This is parity in the sense of Mitchell et al., a comparison against the counterfactual,
# not payback in the sense of returning to the pre-removal stock. Both are reported.
crossing <- function(f, horizon = HORIZON) {
  if (f(0) >= 0) return(0)
  if (f(horizon) < 0) return(NA_real_)
  uniroot(f, c(0, horizon), tol = 1e-6)$root
}

parity_time <- function(p) {
  crossing(function(t) C_remove(t, p$C_inv, p$D, p$C_nat, p$r_nat) -
                       C_leave(t, p$C_inv, p$K_inv, p$r_inv))
}

payback_time <- function(p) {
  crossing(function(t) C_remove(t, p$C_inv, p$D, p$C_nat, p$r_nat) - p$C_inv)
}

# Net carbon benefit of removal relative to leaving the invader in place, at time t.
# This is the quantity a project would claim, and it is negative for as long as the
# removal trajectory sits below the counterfactual.
net_benefit <- function(t, p) {
  C_remove(t, p$C_inv, p$D, p$C_nat, p$r_nat) - C_leave(t, p$C_inv, p$K_inv, p$r_inv)
}

# Rate constant implied by a chronosequence: a state observed at C_t after t years of
# recovery from C_0 toward an asymptote K. Used where a source reports a recovery
# observation rather than a rate.
rate_from_chrono <- function(C0, Ct, K, t) {
  if (any(!is.finite(c(C0, Ct, K, t))) || K <= Ct || K <= C0) return(NA_real_)
  -log((K - Ct) / (K - C0)) / t
}
# Assemble the point estimate parameter set for each system from the long table.
PARNAMES <- c("C_inv", "C_nat", "AGB_inv", "K_inv", "r_inv", "r_nat",
              "f_rel", "dSOC", "E_op")

pars_point <- lapply(SYS, function(sid) {
  p <- as.list(setNames(sapply(PARNAMES, function(x) getp(sid, x)), PARNAMES))
  # where a source gives no invaded asymptote the invaded state is treated as at
  # equilibrium, which is the conservative assumption for the removal case
  if (!is.finite(p$K_inv)) { p$K_inv <- p$C_inv; p$r_inv <- 0 }
  if (!is.finite(p$r_inv)) p$r_inv <- 0
  p$D <- debt(p$AGB_inv, p$f_rel, p$dSOC, p$E_op)
  p
})
names(pars_point) <- SYS

# Point estimate results
res_point <- do.call(rbind, lapply(SYS, function(sid) {
  p <- pars_point[[sid]]
  data.frame(
    system_id = sid,
    debt      = p$D,
    parity    = parity_time(p),
    payback   = payback_time(p),
    nb40      = net_benefit(CREDIT, p),
    nb100     = net_benefit(100, p),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
rownames(res_point) <- NULL
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Uncertainty
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every parameter is drawn from a normal distribution centred on its point estimate
# with the dispersion its source reports. Where a source reports a standard error and a
# sample size the standard deviation is recovered as SE * sqrt(n); where it reports no
# dispersion at all the parameter is given a coefficient of variation of 0.20, and the
# consequence of that choice is examined in the sensitivity analysis. Stocks and rates
# are truncated at zero, and f_rel is truncated to the unit interval, because negative
# stocks and negative release fractions are not physically meaningful.

draw_sd <- function(sid, p) {
  s <- getp(sid, p, "sd")
  n <- getp(sid, p, "n")
  v <- getp(sid, p, "value")
  if (is.finite(s)) {
    # sources reporting a standard error alongside n are converted to a standard deviation
    if (identical(par_long$disp[par_long$system_id == sid & par_long$parameter == p][1], "se") &&
        is.finite(n)) return(s * sqrt(n))
    return(s)
  }
  abs(v) * DEFAULT_CV
}

rtrunc <- function(n, mean, sd, lo = 0, hi = Inf) {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean, sd)
  x[x < lo] <- lo
  x[x > hi] <- hi
  x
}

simulate_system <- function(sid, nsim = NSIM) {
  p0 <- pars_point[[sid]]
  d  <- list()
  for (nm in c("C_inv", "C_nat", "AGB_inv", "dSOC", "E_op")) {
    d[[nm]] <- rtrunc(nsim, p0[[nm]], draw_sd(sid, nm))
  }
  d$r_nat <- rtrunc(nsim, p0$r_nat, draw_sd(sid, "r_nat"), lo = 1e-6)
  d$f_rel <- rtrunc(nsim, p0$f_rel, draw_sd(sid, "f_rel"), lo = 0, hi = 1)
  d$K_inv <- if (identical(p0$K_inv, p0$C_inv)) d$C_inv else
             rtrunc(nsim, p0$K_inv, draw_sd(sid, "K_inv"))
  d$r_inv <- rep(p0$r_inv, nsim)

  out <- data.frame(parity = numeric(nsim), payback = numeric(nsim), nb40 = numeric(nsim))
  for (i in seq_len(nsim)) {
    p <- list(C_inv = d$C_inv[i], C_nat = d$C_nat[i], K_inv = d$K_inv[i],
              r_inv = d$r_inv[i], r_nat = d$r_nat[i])
    p$D <- debt(d$AGB_inv[i], d$f_rel[i], d$dSOC[i], d$E_op[i])
    out$parity[i]  <- parity_time(p)
    out$payback[i] <- payback_time(p)
    out$nb40[i]    <- net_benefit(CREDIT, p)
  }
  out
}

sims <- lapply(SYS, simulate_system)
names(sims) <- SYS

# summarise: median and 95 percent interval of parity time among draws that reach parity,
# and the probability that parity is never reached inside the 300 year horizon
res_mc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(SYS, function(sid) {
  s  <- sims[[sid]]
  ok <- is.finite(s$parity)
  q  <- if (any(ok)) quantile(s$parity[ok], c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)) else rep(NA_real_, 3)
  data.frame(system_id = sid,
             p_never   = mean(!ok),
             parity_lo = q[1], parity_md = q[2], parity_hi = q[3],
             nb40_md   = median(s$nb40),
             nb40_lo   = quantile(s$nb40, 0.025),
             nb40_hi   = quantile(s$nb40, 0.975),
             p_nb40_neg = mean(s$nb40 < 0),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
rownames(res_mc) <- NULL

res <- merge(merge(sysmeta, res_point, by = "system_id"), res_mc, by = "system_id")
res <- res[order(res$display_order), ]
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The crediting test
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two questions decide whether a removal project could be credited at all under the
# accounting rules the standards actually use.
#
# 1. Does the project generate a positive net benefit inside the crediting period? If
#    the removal trajectory is still below the counterfactual at year 40, there is
#    nothing to credit no matter how the rules are written.
# 2. Is the removal debt small enough to be waved through as de minimis? Verra permits
#    an omitted decrease in carbon stocks only where it is below 5 percent of the total
#    greenhouse gas benefit the project generates. A removal whose debt exceeds that
#    share of its own benefit must account for the debt explicitly, and no approved
#    methodology outside the matched baseline design provides a way to do so.

res$claimable   <- res$nb40_md > 0
res$debt_share  <- ifelse(res$nb40_md > 0, res$debt / res$nb40_md, NA_real_)
res$deminimis   <- is.finite(res$debt_share) & res$debt_share < DEMINIMIS
res$verdict <- ifelse(!res$claimable, "no claimable benefit at 40 yr",
               ifelse(res$deminimis,  "claimable, debt de minimis",
                                      "claimable, debt must be accounted"))

# headline values, defined here because the abstract quotes them and inline R is evaluated
# in document order
maxdebt   <- res$system_short[which.max(res$debt)]
maxdebt_v <- max(res$debt)
mindebt_v <- min(res$debt)
aud <- read.csv(file.path(IN, "standards-audit.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
CRIT <- c(introduce_prohibited   = "Introduction prohibited",
          removal_named_eligible = "Removal a named eligible activity",
          removal_creditable_carbon = "Carbon effect of removal creditable",
          biomass_debt_resolved  = "Invader biomass debt resolved",
          species_named          = "Any invasive taxon named",
          creditable_non_carbon  = "Removal creditable under a non carbon instrument")

audm <- reshape(aud[, c("standard_short", "criterion", "code")],
                idvar = "standard_short", timevar = "criterion", direction = "wide")
names(audm) <- sub("^code\\.", "", names(audm))
audm <- audm[, c("standard_short", names(CRIT))]
STORD <- c("Verra", "Plan Vivo", "Gold Standard", "ACR", "CAR", "Article 6.4", "ACCU")
audm <- audm[match(STORD, audm$standard_short), ]
rownames(audm) <- NULL

Abstract

Removing an invasive plant is one of the few restoration actions with an unambiguous biodiversity rationale and no reliable way to pay for it. Carbon finance fails it for a reason that is arithmetic rather than administrative: a woody invader is itself a carbon stock, so clearing it registers as an emission against a carbon-rich baseline and meets, on its face, every test for baseline gaming. Whether removal is nevertheless a carbon gain depends on a quantity that has not been estimated, the time for recovering native vegetation to overtake the trajectory the invader would have followed if left in place. We adapt the carbon parity framework developed for biofuel and bioenergy accounting to invasive plant removal and apply it to 7 invaded systems spanning woody nitrogen-fixing invaders, a thicket-forming shrub, an annual grass, a wetland graminoid, a woody wetland tree and a floating aquatic. Removal debts span 0.4 to 51.0 Mg C per hectare and parity times run from immediate to never, ordered by the functional type of the invader. Only 2 systems can be parameterised entirely from measurement, which is itself a finding: the recovery rate that dominates the calculation is the quantity the literature measures least. We then audit six voluntary carbon standards and one compliance scheme against their own current requirement documents. All restrict the introduction of invasive species, none credits the carbon consequence of removing them, and the one design that dissolves the problem, the dynamic matched baseline, is confined to forest in a single country. The activity is monetised only as biochar feedstock and as a biodiversity credit, neither of which rewards the land carbon effect. The parity calculation, not the standards text, should decide where carbon finance is the right instrument, and for much of the invaded world it is not.

1. Introduction

Invasive alien species are among the recognised direct drivers of biodiversity loss, and the first global assessment devoted to them concluded that they are also among the most expensive, with costs that have risen steeply over recent decades (Diagne et al., 2021; IPBES, 2023). The international response has set targets for their control, but the financing to meet those targets has no obvious source. The Kunming-Montreal framework asks parties to reduce the introduction and establishment of invasive species and, separately, to restore a substantial share of degraded ecosystems, while relying on private finance to help pay for both (Convention on Biological Diversity, 2022).

Restoration finance has consolidated around carbon, and invasive removal fits that instrument badly. Almost every other restoration action adds something: trees, wetland, soil carbon, structural complexity. Removal takes something away, and in the case of a woody invader what it takes away is biomass carbon that a carbon accountant is obliged to count. A proponent who clears a dense stand of an invasive tree has, on the face of the ledger, done what the market is designed to prevent. The clearing is deliberate, it is carried out by the proponent, and it is motivated by carbon finance. Those three facts are the standard test for baseline gaming, and a genuine restoration project satisfies all of them.

The scientific question underneath the accounting question has been answered only in fragments. A substantial literature quantifies what invasion does to ecosystem carbon, beginning with the finding that invasion alters carbon and nitrogen pools systematically and often upward (Liao et al., 2008; Peltzer, Allen, Lovett, Whitehead, & Wardle, 2010; Vilà et al., 2011), and continuing into mechanism through soil biota, microbial biomass and heterotrophic respiration (He et al., 2025; Negesse et al., 2025; Raheem et al., 2024). A much thinner literature follows what happens after removal, and it is dominated by endpoints other than carbon. The most recent global synthesis of post-removal revegetation reports native cover recovering by nearly half and non-native cover falling by more than a quarter, with carbon appearing only as an ordering claim, that abundance recovers faster than carbon stocks, which recover faster than diversity (Ahmad et al., 2026). The two halves have never been joined into the quantity a financing decision requires, which is the time the removal trajectory takes to overtake the counterfactual.

That quantity has a well developed analogue. Biofuel accounting confronted the same structure when it became clear that clearing native vegetation for an energy crop incurs an immediate carbon debt that the crop’s annual savings must repay, with payback periods running to centuries in the worst cases (Fargione, Hill, Tilman, Polasky, & Hawthorne, 2008; Searchinger et al., 2008). Forest bioenergy accounting then sharpened the idea by separating payback, the return to the pre-intervention stock, from parity, the point at which the intervention overtakes the trajectory the stand would otherwise have followed (Mitchell, Harmon, & O’Connell, 2012). Parity, not payback, is the quantity relevant to a counterfactual-based crediting system, and it is the quantity computed here. The same literature is candid about the framework’s fragility, since methodological choices alone can move parity estimates by two orders of magnitude (Jonker, Junginger, & Faaij, 2014), which is why the accounting boundary and the counterfactual are fixed here before any result is computed.

The nearest existing treatment of invasive control as climate action concerns invasive mammals on islands (Honzák et al., 2024), where the eradication target holds no standing biomass and the accounting problem examined here never arises. That asymmetry between animal and woody-plant invaders is the gap this paper occupies.

Three questions follow. First, across invaded systems that differ in the functional type of the invader, how long is the time to carbon parity after removal, and in which systems is it never reached? Second, given those answers, could a removal project be credited under the accounting rules that carbon standards actually apply? Third, where the carbon answer is unfavourable, what instrument is appropriate instead?

2. Methods

2.1 Systems and the evidence base

t1 <- sysmeta[order(sysmeta$display_order),
              c("system_short", "invader", "region", "functional_type", "evidence_class")]
names(t1) <- c("System", "Invader", "Region", "Functional type", "Evidence")
kable(t1, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(t1, file.path(TBL, "table-1-systems.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

Systems were selected to span the functional types across which the carbon consequence of removal is expected to differ, rather than to be a representative sample of invaded ecosystems, which the available data would not support. The selection is deliberately adversarial to the framing advanced here: it includes the systems in which removal is most likely to be a carbon loss as well as those in which it is most likely to be a gain.

The evidence classification in Table 1 is derived from the parameter tiers rather than asserted, so a system counts as quantified only where both ecosystem stocks and the invader’s own aboveground carbon come from measurement or from arithmetic on measurements. On that test 2 of the 7 systems are quantified and 5 are indicative. That ratio is itself a result. It is not possible at present to assemble a fully measured parity calculation for most of the world’s best known plant invasions, and the reader should treat the indicative systems as showing the sign and rough magnitude of an effect rather than its value.

2.2 The parity model

The model compares two futures from the moment of intervention. Under the leave scenario the invader is retained and total ecosystem carbon relaxes toward the asymptote of the invaded state. Under the remove scenario the stock falls instantaneously by the removal debt, then relaxes toward the native reference stock at the rate at which native vegetation reaccumulates carbon on cleared ground. Both trajectories take the monomolecular form, which is the standard representation of stock recovery toward a carrying capacity and requires only a starting stock, an asymptote and a rate constant.

The removal debt has three components: the fraction of the invader’s own aboveground carbon released to the atmosphere within a year of clearing, any soil organic carbon lost to the disturbance itself, and the operational emissions of the clearing work. Carbon that leaves the site in durable form, as timber or biochar, is not part of the debt, which is why the biochar route discussed below changes the arithmetic rather than merely the finance.

Carbon parity is the first time at which the removal trajectory crosses the leave trajectory. Payback, reported alongside it, is the first time at which the removal trajectory returns to the pre-removal stock. The two differ whenever the invaded state is not at equilibrium, and the difference matters because a crediting system pays for the former while intuition tends to reach for the latter.

2.3 Parameterisation and uncertainty

t2 <- par_long[, c("system_id", "parameter", "value", "sd", "n", "units", "source_key", "tier")]
t2 <- t2[order(match(t2$system_id, sysmeta$system_id[order(sysmeta$display_order)]),
               match(t2$parameter, PARNAMES)), ]
names(t2) <- c("System", "Parameter", "Value", "SD", "n", "Units", "Source", "Tier")
kable(t2, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)
write.csv(t2, file.path(TBL, "table-2-parameters.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
tier_tab <- table(factor(par_long$tier, levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D")))
n_tierD  <- as.integer(tier_tab["D"])
n_par    <- nrow(par_long)

Of the 49 parameters entering the model, 5 are measured with a reported dispersion, 2 are measured point estimates, 4 are derived by arithmetic set out in the code above, and 38 are transferred from another system or taken as a global default. The last group is concentrated in the recovery rate, which is the least measured and most influential parameter in the model, a point we return to.

Uncertainty is propagated by Monte Carlo with 10,000 draws per system. Each parameter is drawn from a normal distribution centred on its point estimate, truncated where the physical meaning requires it, with the dispersion its source reports. Where a source reports none, the parameter is assigned a coefficient of variation of 0.20, and the sensitivity of the conclusions to that assumption is examined directly.

2.4 Standards audit

Six crediting regimes were audited against their own current requirement documents rather than against summaries: the Verra Verified Carbon Standard together with the Climate, Community and Biodiversity Standards, Plan Vivo, the Gold Standard, the American Carbon Registry, the Climate Action Reserve, and the Article 6.4 mechanism of the Paris Agreement. The Australian Carbon Credit Unit scheme was added as the one compliance regime in which suppression of non-native plants appears in statute. Each document was retrieved, its full text searched for the relevant terms, and each occurrence read in context, because the phrase appears in a great many project documents as a compliance negation, a statement that invasive species will not be introduced, which is the opposite of the activity at issue.

3. Results

3.1 Time to carbon parity

# values quoted in this section, computed rather than typed
res_ok    <- res[is.finite(res$parity_md), ]
res_never <- res[res$p_never > 0.5, ]
fastest   <- res_ok$system_short[which.min(res_ok$parity_md)]
fastest_t <- min(res_ok$parity_md, na.rm = TRUE)
slowest   <- res_ok$system_short[which.max(res_ok$parity_md)]
slowest_t <- max(res_ok$parity_md, na.rm = TRUE)
n_neg40   <- sum(res$nb40_md < 0)

Removal debts span 0.4 to 51.0 Mg C per hectare, a range of more than an order of magnitude, and they order the systems almost exactly as the functional type of the invader would predict. The largest debt falls on Everglades wetland, where the invader is itself the dominant carbon pool of the system, and the smallest on systems where the invader holds negligible standing biomass and its effect on carbon runs through suppression of the native community rather than through its own stock.

Parity times follow from that ordering but not proportionally, because repayment depends on the gap between the native asymptote and the invaded stock rather than on the debt alone. Among systems that reach parity at all, the range runs from 5 years in Dry deciduous forest to 49 years in Everglades wetland. 4 of the 7 systems do not reach parity within the three-century horizon in the majority of Monte Carlo draws, and 4 are still below the counterfactual at the end of a forty year crediting period.

t3 <- data.frame(
  System    = res$system_short,
  `Debt (Mg C/ha)` = f1(res$debt),
  `Parity (yr)` = ifelse(res$p_never > 0.5, "not reached",
                    paste0(yr(res$parity_md), " (", yr(res$parity_lo), "-", yr(res$parity_hi), ")")),
  `P(never)` = pc(res$p_never),
  `Payback (yr)` = yr(res$payback),
  `Net benefit at 40 yr (Mg C/ha)` = paste0(f1(res$nb40_md), " (", f1(res$nb40_lo), " to ", f1(res$nb40_hi), ")"),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(t3, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(t3, file.path(TBL, "table-3-parity.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
png(file.path(FIG, "figure-1-concept.png"), width = 2700, height = 1260, res = 300)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.6, 2.4, 1.2), family = "sans", cex.axis = 0.9)

3.2 Sensitivity

# One at a time elasticity: the proportional change in parity time produced by a ten
# percent increase in each parameter, holding the rest at their point estimates. Where
# parity is not reached at either the base or the perturbed value the elasticity is
# undefined and reported as such.
#
# One subtlety has to be handled explicitly. Where a source gives no invaded asymptote the
# assembly step sets K_inv equal to C_inv, so the retention trajectory is flat. Perturbing
# C_inv alone would then leave a stale K_inv below the new starting stock and the retention
# curve would bend downward, which is an artefact of the perturbation rather than a property
# of the system. K_inv is therefore moved with C_inv wherever the two were tied.
static_invaded <- sapply(SYS, function(s) isTRUE(all.equal(pars_point[[s]]$K_inv,
                                                           pars_point[[s]]$C_inv)))
names(static_invaded) <- SYS

elasticity <- function(sid, p_name, delta = 0.10) {
  p0 <- pars_point[[sid]]
  t0 <- parity_time(p0)
  p1 <- p0
  p1[[p_name]] <- p0[[p_name]] * (1 + delta)
  if (p_name == "C_inv" && static_invaded[[sid]]) p1$K_inv <- p1$C_inv
  p1$D <- debt(p1$AGB_inv, p1$f_rel, p1$dSOC, p1$E_op)
  t1 <- parity_time(p1)
  if (!is.finite(t0) || !is.finite(t1) || t0 == 0) return(NA_real_)
  ((t1 - t0) / t0) / delta
}

ELP <- c("C_nat", "r_nat", "AGB_inv", "f_rel", "dSOC", "C_inv")
# short axis labels; the full parameter definitions are in Table 2
ELLAB <- c(C_nat = "Native stock", r_nat = "Recovery rate", AGB_inv = "Invader AGB",
           f_rel = "Released fraction", dSOC = "Soil C loss", C_inv = "Invaded stock")
elas <- outer(SYS, ELP, Vectorize(function(s, p) elasticity(s, p)))
dimnames(elas) <- list(sysmeta$system_short[match(SYS, sysmeta$system_id)], ELP)

The parity time is most sensitive to C_nat, with a mean absolute elasticity of 3.13 across systems, and second most sensitive to C_inv at 2.15. An elasticity of one means that a ten per cent change in the parameter moves the parity time by ten per cent. Elasticities on the recovery rate are negative throughout, as they must be, since faster native reaccumulation shortens the time to parity. Elasticities on the invader’s own aboveground stock and on the released fraction are positive, since both enlarge the debt.

The practical consequence is uncomfortable. The parameter that matters most is the one the literature measures least. Standing stocks in invaded and uninvaded states are widely reported, frequently with dispersion and sample sizes, whereas the rate at which native vegetation reaccumulates carbon after clearance is reported almost nowhere, and where it is reported it comes from a chronosequence rather than a time series.

All 7 regimes restrict the introduction of invasive species, 7 of them with an explicit prohibition or an equivalent requirement. 4 name removal somewhere as an eligible or permitted activity. 0 provide a route by which the carbon consequence of removal is itself credited. 1 resolve the accounting problem that clearing a woody invader creates, and the one that does resolves it by assumption rather than by measurement, placing the emissions of required weed removal outside the project boundary on the ground that removal would have happened anyway.

The asymmetry between the columns is the finding. The obligation runs one way throughout. A proponent may be required to demonstrate that invasive populations have not increased, and may in some regimes be encouraged to eradicate, while having no mechanism by which the carbon result of doing so can be quantified or paid for. 2 of the regimes credit removal under a non-carbon instrument, scoring invasive abundance as a biodiversity outcome, which is the only place in the voluntary market where the activity is currently rewarded on its own terms.

3.4 Where the parity answer and the crediting answer meet

t5 <- data.frame(
  System = res$system_short,
  `Claimable at 40 yr` = ifelse(res$claimable, "yes", "no"),
  # a debt share far above 100 per cent means the benefit is near zero rather than that the
  # debt is unusually large, so the ratio is capped for display and read with the benefit column
  `Debt as share of benefit` = ifelse(!is.finite(res$debt_share), "-",
                               ifelse(res$debt_share > 10, "over 1000%", pc(res$debt_share))),
  `Passes de minimis` = ifelse(is.na(res$deminimis), "-", ifelse(res$deminimis, "yes", "no")),
  Verdict = res$verdict,
  `Available route` = res$route,
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(t5, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(t5, file.path(TBL, "table-5-verdict.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

Joining the two analyses narrows the field sharply. A removal project needs three things at once: a positive net benefit inside the crediting period, a debt small enough that the accounting rules can absorb it, and a methodology whose baseline construction does not penalise the proponent for the invader’s own biomass. Table 5 shows how few systems hold all three. The systems that pass the carbon test tend to be those where the invader holds least carbon, which are also the systems where a carbon-denominated payment would be smallest, and the systems where removal delivers the largest ecological gain tend to fail it.

4. Discussion

# values quoted in the discussion, computed rather than typed
n_never    <- sum(res$p_never > 0.5)
n_fast     <- sum(is.finite(res$parity_md) & res$parity_md <= 20)
n_claim    <- sum(res$claimable)
n_dem      <- sum(res$deminimis, na.rm = TRUE)
worst      <- res$system_short[which.min(res$nb40_md)]
best       <- res$system_short[which.max(res$nb40_md)]
span_lo    <- min(res$parity_md, na.rm = TRUE)
span_hi    <- max(res$parity_md, na.rm = TRUE)
r_nat_elas <- mean(abs(elas[, "r_nat"]), na.rm = TRUE)
agb_elas   <- mean(abs(elas[, "AGB_inv"]), na.rm = TRUE)

4.1 The answer depends on what kind of invader it is

The parity times reported here span a range wide enough that no general statement about the carbon consequence of invasive removal can be defended. Of the seven systems, 4 do not reach parity at all within three centuries, while 2 reach it within twenty years. The ordering follows the functional type of the invader almost perfectly, and it follows it for a reason that the model makes explicit. The debt scales with the aboveground carbon the invader holds, and the repayment scales with the difference between the native asymptote and the invaded stock. An invader that holds little carbon and suppresses a system capable of holding a great deal is cheap to remove and repays quickly. An invader that is itself the largest carbon pool in the system, and that has displaced vegetation of comparable or lower stock, cannot be removed at a carbon profit on any horizon a crediting period can reach.

This is why the woody nitrogen-fixing invaders are the hard case and the annual grasses are the easy one, and it is why the wetland graminoid is hardest of all. Where an invader outperforms the native community it displaced, as the evidence for Phragmites soil carbon in several North American marshes indicates (Campbell & Campbell, 2026; J. Gu, Ardenne, & Chmura, 2020), the removal trajectory never crosses the counterfactual and the parity framework returns not a long time but no time at all. The finding for invasive acacias in Atlantic Forest regrowth is the same result in a forest setting: carbon accumulates roughly three times faster under the invader while phylogenetic and functional diversity recovery collapses (Matos et al., 2023).

That result should not be read as an argument against removal. It is an argument against carbon as the instrument that pays for it. The systems in which removal costs the most carbon are frequently the systems in which it delivers the most biodiversity, which is precisely the trade-off the acacia work quantifies. A financing mechanism that ranks restoration actions by carbon will systematically defund the removals with the strongest ecological case.

4.2 The standards cannot express the answer, in either direction

The audit returns a uniform result across regimes that otherwise share very little. All 7 prohibit or discourage the introduction of invasive species. 4 name removal as an eligible or permitted activity somewhere in their documents. 0 provide a route by which the carbon consequence of removal can itself be credited. The obligation is negative throughout: do not introduce, do not let populations rise. Nowhere in the voluntary market is there an instrument that asks whether removing an established invader would be a carbon gain, because nowhere is there an instrument that could act on the answer.

Two features of the current rules make this more than an omission. The first is that clearing pre-existing woody biomass is tested against a rule written to catch baseline gaming, and a genuine removal project fails that test on its face. Verra’s own consultation record shows proponents asking what threshold of clearing is permissible and being told that no quantitative threshold exists, with the answer falling back on a de minimis allowance that requires the omitted decrease to stay below five per cent of the project’s total benefit. Of the systems examined here, 3 generate a positive benefit inside a forty year crediting period at all, and 0 of those carry a debt small enough to pass that test. For the remainder, the debt must be accounted explicitly, and no approved methodology outside the matched baseline design provides a way to do so.

The second is that the eligibility machinery has been built while the quantification machinery has not. Verra’s tidal wetland methodology has listed the removal of invasive species as an eligible activity since 2015, and the programme standard has carried an eligibility route for land whose dominant cover is an invasive species threatening ecosystem health. A proponent can therefore establish that a site qualifies and then discover there is no way to quantify what the project does to it. The recent tightening of that route, from a blanket exemption to an evidentiary test requiring a defined dominance threshold, sharpens the mismatch rather than resolving it.

4.3 One accounting design already dissolves the problem

The dynamic matched baseline is the exception, and it appears not to have been recognised as one. Where the counterfactual is constructed from matched control plots rather than modelled forward from the project site, the invader stands in both the project and the control. Its removal is then not an emission against the baseline, because the baseline contains it too, and the credit attaches to the differential growth of the regeneration that removal releases. The problem that defeats every other methodology is dissolved by the structure of the comparison rather than by an exemption.

The constraint on that design is jurisdictional and structural, not conceptual. It requires a national forest inventory dense enough to supply matched controls, which at present means the conterminous United States, and it requires forest that remains forest, which excludes every marsh, rangeland and open ecosystem in this study. Extending matched baselines to non-forest biomes is a tractable research programme with an existing template, and it is the single change that would do most to make invasive removal creditable where removal actually pays.

Two routes already monetise the activity, and it is worth being precise about what they pay for. Converting cleared invasive biomass to biochar moves the carbon from the land pool to a durable pool, so the land carbon loss is compensated rather than avoided, which is why the biochar route changes the arithmetic and not merely the finance. Crediting invasive control as a biodiversity outcome, as Verra’s nature framework and Plan Vivo’s nature standard both now do, pays for the ecological result directly and never touches the carbon question. Neither rewards the land carbon effect of removal, and on the evidence assembled here, for most systems neither should.

4.4 What the sensitivity analysis says about the evidence base

The parity time is most sensitive to the native recovery rate, with a mean absolute elasticity of 0.91 across systems, and considerably less sensitive to the invader’s aboveground stock, at 0.83. This ordering is inconvenient, because the recovery rate is the parameter the literature measures least. Post-removal carbon trajectories are rare in every system examined here, and outside the Kenyan rangeland chronosequence there is essentially no multi-decadal observation of carbon reaccumulation after invasive plant clearance anywhere in the world.

The most striking instance is the largest invasive removal programme on earth. South Africa’s Working for Water has cleared invasive trees at national scale for three decades with monitoring effort directed at water yield, employment and vegetation recovery (Wilgen et al., 2012; Wilgen & Wannenburgh, 2016). It is almost entirely carbon-blind, and it is therefore unable to answer, for the fynbos and grassland catchments it has treated, the question this paper poses. That is a recommendation rather than a limitation. A carbon measurement programme retrofitted onto existing Working for Water clearance chronosequences would produce the single most valuable dataset in this field at a fraction of the cost of establishing new sites.

4.5 Limitations

The model is deliberately simple. Both trajectories are monomolecular approaches to an asymptote, which represents stock recovery adequately but cannot represent a system that overshoots, collapses, or is reinvaded. Secondary invasion after clearing is common and is not modelled; where it occurs, the real parity times will be longer than those reported here and in some systems parity will be lost entirely.

The accounting boundary is carbon stock only. Three consequences follow. Methane and nitrous oxide are excluded, which matters most in the wetland and aquatic systems, where the flux literature is unresolved and in the case of floating aquatics the stock framing may be the wrong one altogether (Z. Gu et al., 2025; Martin & Moseman-Valtierra, 2017). Fire regime feedbacks are excluded, which understates the case for removing invasive annual grasses, since the invasion-fire cycle removes carbon that a stock comparison of unburned states does not see. And the durable-product fate of cleared biomass is treated as a parameter rather than a scenario.

The transferred parameters are concentrated where they do most damage. Recovery rates for four of seven systems are taken from analogues rather than measured in the system itself, and those systems are reported as indicative rather than quantified throughout. Sensitivity to the assumed dispersion of unreported parameters was tested directly and does not change the ordering of systems, but it does widen the intervals, and the intervals are wide already.

Finally, the parity framework inherits a known fragility. In the bioenergy literature, methodological choices alone swing payback times from under a year to twenty-seven and parity from two years to more than a century (Jonker et al., 2014). Fixing the accounting boundary and the counterfactual before computing anything, as done here, contains that problem without eliminating it, and cross-study comparison of parity times should be treated with the same caution the bioenergy literature learned to apply.

5. Conclusion

The question of whether invasive plant removal is a carbon gain has an answer, and the answer is that it depends on the invader in a way that is predictable from its functional type and computable from data that already exists for some systems and conspicuously does not for others. Where the invader holds little carbon and suppresses a system capable of holding much, removal repays quickly. Where the invader is the dominant carbon pool, removal does not repay on any horizon a crediting period can reach, and in the systems where the invader outperforms the community it displaced, it does not repay at all.

The carbon standards cannot act on that answer in either direction. They have built the eligibility machinery for invaded land while leaving the quantification machinery unbuilt, and the one accounting design that dissolves the underlying problem is confined to forest in a single country. The result is an activity that is simultaneously required as a safeguard, named as eligible, and impossible to credit.

Two things follow. The narrow one is technical: extending dynamic matched baselines beyond forest would make removal creditable in the systems where the parity calculation says it should be. The broader one is that carbon is the wrong lens for most of this work. The systems where removal costs the most carbon are often those where it delivers the most biodiversity, and a mechanism that ranks restoration by carbon will defund exactly the removals with the strongest ecological case. The emerging biodiversity credit instruments, which already score invasive abundance directly, are the better fit. The parity calculation should decide which instrument applies, and for a large share of the invaded world it says the answer is not carbon.

Data availability

Every parameter entering the analysis, its dispersion, its units and the source it was read from is given in Table 2 and held in 02.inputs/carbon-parameters.csv. The standards audit, including the clause and the document version each code was read from, is held in 02.inputs/standards-audit.csv. Rendering the manuscript reruns the entire analysis from those two files and regenerates every table and figure, so no result reported here exists outside the code that produced it. The manuscript source, the input tables and the code are archived together and require no software beyond R and base packages.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: true
#| output: false

# Rendering this manuscript runs the entire analysis. Every number in the text, every
# table and every figure below is produced by the R code in this document, so the prose
# and the results cannot drift apart. Nothing is fetched over the network: both inputs
# are parameter tables held in 02.inputs, each row carrying the source it was read from.
# Base R only, no packages beyond knitr, so the document renders on any R installation.

library(knitr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)

repo <- normalizePath("..")
IN   <- file.path(repo, "02.inputs")
TBL  <- file.path(repo, "03.outputs", "tables")
FIG  <- file.path(repo, "03.outputs", "figures")
dir.create(TBL, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(FIG, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(20260730)          # the Monte Carlo below is reproducible from this seed
NSIM      <- 10000          # draws per system
HORIZON   <- 300            # years; parity is reported as not reached beyond this
CREDIT    <- 40             # years; the AFOLU crediting period used for the crediting test
DEMINIMIS <- 0.05           # the 5 percent de minimis threshold used by Verra
DEFAULT_CV <- 0.20          # dispersion assumed where a source reports none
CO2_C     <- 44 / 12        # conversion from carbon to carbon dioxide equivalent

# formatting helpers used throughout
f1  <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2  <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f0  <- function(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
pc  <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
yr  <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "not reached", sprintf("%.0f", x))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-parameters
#| echo: true

# The parameter table is long format, one row per parameter per system, so provenance
# travels with the value. Tier A is measured with dispersion, B measured as a point
# estimate, C derived by arithmetic shown in this document, D transferred from another
# system or a global default because nothing system specific exists.
par_long <- read.csv(file.path(IN, "carbon-parameters.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sysmeta  <- read.csv(file.path(IN, "systems.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# any parameter still flagged provisional is a hard stop: the manuscript must not report
# a number that has not been read from a source
prov <- par_long[par_long$tier == "P", ]
if (nrow(prov) > 0) {
  stop("Provisional parameters remain in carbon-parameters.csv: ",
       paste(unique(paste(prov$system_id, prov$parameter)), collapse = ", "))
}

# pull a single parameter for a single system
getp <- function(sid, p, field = "value") {
  r <- par_long[par_long$system_id == sid & par_long$parameter == p, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  as.numeric(r[[field]][1])
}
gett <- function(sid, p) {
  r <- par_long[par_long$system_id == sid & par_long$parameter == p, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(NA_character_)
  r$tier[1]
}

SYS <- sysmeta$system_id
names(SYS) <- sysmeta$system_short

# Evidence class is derived from the parameter tiers rather than asserted in the input file,
# so the manuscript cannot describe a system as quantified unless the parameters say so. A
# system is quantified only where both stocks and the invader's own aboveground carbon are
# measured or derived rather than transferred from elsewhere.
KEYPAR <- c("C_inv", "C_nat", "AGB_inv")
sysmeta$evidence_class <- sapply(sysmeta$system_id, function(s)
  if (all(sapply(KEYPAR, function(p) gett(s, p)) %in% c("A", "B", "C")))
    "Quantified" else "Indicative")
n_quant <- sum(sysmeta$evidence_class == "Quantified")
n_indic <- sum(sysmeta$evidence_class == "Indicative")
```

```{r}
#| label: model-functions
#| echo: true

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The two trajectory parity model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Both scenarios are monomolecular approaches to an asymptote, the standard form for
# stock recovery toward a carrying capacity. C(t) = K - (K - C0) exp(-r t).
#
# LEAVE: the invader is retained. The stock relaxes from the measured invaded stock
# C_inv toward the invaded asymptote K_inv at rate r_inv. Where the invaded state is
# already at equilibrium, K_inv equals C_inv and the trajectory is flat.
#
# REMOVE: at t = 0 the stock falls instantaneously by the removal debt D, then relaxes
# from that reduced starting point toward the native reference stock C_nat at rate
# r_nat, the rate at which native vegetation reaccumulates carbon on cleared ground.

approach <- function(t, C0, K, r) K - (K - C0) * exp(-r * t)

C_leave  <- function(t, C_inv, K_inv, r_inv) approach(t, C_inv, K_inv, r_inv)

# The debt is the carbon the removal puts into the atmosphere, or removes from the site
# without replacing: the released fraction of the invader's own aboveground stock, plus
# any soil carbon lost to the disturbance, plus the operational emissions of clearing.
debt <- function(AGB_inv, f_rel, dSOC, E_op) AGB_inv * f_rel + dSOC + E_op

C_remove <- function(t, C_inv, D, C_nat, r_nat) approach(t, C_inv - D, C_nat, r_nat)

# Carbon parity is the first time the removal trajectory catches the leave trajectory.
# This is parity in the sense of Mitchell et al., a comparison against the counterfactual,
# not payback in the sense of returning to the pre-removal stock. Both are reported.
crossing <- function(f, horizon = HORIZON) {
  if (f(0) >= 0) return(0)
  if (f(horizon) < 0) return(NA_real_)
  uniroot(f, c(0, horizon), tol = 1e-6)$root
}

parity_time <- function(p) {
  crossing(function(t) C_remove(t, p$C_inv, p$D, p$C_nat, p$r_nat) -
                       C_leave(t, p$C_inv, p$K_inv, p$r_inv))
}

payback_time <- function(p) {
  crossing(function(t) C_remove(t, p$C_inv, p$D, p$C_nat, p$r_nat) - p$C_inv)
}

# Net carbon benefit of removal relative to leaving the invader in place, at time t.
# This is the quantity a project would claim, and it is negative for as long as the
# removal trajectory sits below the counterfactual.
net_benefit <- function(t, p) {
  C_remove(t, p$C_inv, p$D, p$C_nat, p$r_nat) - C_leave(t, p$C_inv, p$K_inv, p$r_inv)
}

# Rate constant implied by a chronosequence: a state observed at C_t after t years of
# recovery from C_0 toward an asymptote K. Used where a source reports a recovery
# observation rather than a rate.
rate_from_chrono <- function(C0, Ct, K, t) {
  if (any(!is.finite(c(C0, Ct, K, t))) || K <= Ct || K <= C0) return(NA_real_)
  -log((K - Ct) / (K - C0)) / t
}
```

```{r}
#| label: assemble-parameters
#| echo: true

# Assemble the point estimate parameter set for each system from the long table.
PARNAMES <- c("C_inv", "C_nat", "AGB_inv", "K_inv", "r_inv", "r_nat",
              "f_rel", "dSOC", "E_op")

pars_point <- lapply(SYS, function(sid) {
  p <- as.list(setNames(sapply(PARNAMES, function(x) getp(sid, x)), PARNAMES))
  # where a source gives no invaded asymptote the invaded state is treated as at
  # equilibrium, which is the conservative assumption for the removal case
  if (!is.finite(p$K_inv)) { p$K_inv <- p$C_inv; p$r_inv <- 0 }
  if (!is.finite(p$r_inv)) p$r_inv <- 0
  p$D <- debt(p$AGB_inv, p$f_rel, p$dSOC, p$E_op)
  p
})
names(pars_point) <- SYS

# Point estimate results
res_point <- do.call(rbind, lapply(SYS, function(sid) {
  p <- pars_point[[sid]]
  data.frame(
    system_id = sid,
    debt      = p$D,
    parity    = parity_time(p),
    payback   = payback_time(p),
    nb40      = net_benefit(CREDIT, p),
    nb100     = net_benefit(100, p),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
rownames(res_point) <- NULL
```

```{r}
#| label: monte-carlo
#| echo: true

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Uncertainty
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every parameter is drawn from a normal distribution centred on its point estimate
# with the dispersion its source reports. Where a source reports a standard error and a
# sample size the standard deviation is recovered as SE * sqrt(n); where it reports no
# dispersion at all the parameter is given a coefficient of variation of 0.20, and the
# consequence of that choice is examined in the sensitivity analysis. Stocks and rates
# are truncated at zero, and f_rel is truncated to the unit interval, because negative
# stocks and negative release fractions are not physically meaningful.

draw_sd <- function(sid, p) {
  s <- getp(sid, p, "sd")
  n <- getp(sid, p, "n")
  v <- getp(sid, p, "value")
  if (is.finite(s)) {
    # sources reporting a standard error alongside n are converted to a standard deviation
    if (identical(par_long$disp[par_long$system_id == sid & par_long$parameter == p][1], "se") &&
        is.finite(n)) return(s * sqrt(n))
    return(s)
  }
  abs(v) * DEFAULT_CV
}

rtrunc <- function(n, mean, sd, lo = 0, hi = Inf) {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean, sd)
  x[x < lo] <- lo
  x[x > hi] <- hi
  x
}

simulate_system <- function(sid, nsim = NSIM) {
  p0 <- pars_point[[sid]]
  d  <- list()
  for (nm in c("C_inv", "C_nat", "AGB_inv", "dSOC", "E_op")) {
    d[[nm]] <- rtrunc(nsim, p0[[nm]], draw_sd(sid, nm))
  }
  d$r_nat <- rtrunc(nsim, p0$r_nat, draw_sd(sid, "r_nat"), lo = 1e-6)
  d$f_rel <- rtrunc(nsim, p0$f_rel, draw_sd(sid, "f_rel"), lo = 0, hi = 1)
  d$K_inv <- if (identical(p0$K_inv, p0$C_inv)) d$C_inv else
             rtrunc(nsim, p0$K_inv, draw_sd(sid, "K_inv"))
  d$r_inv <- rep(p0$r_inv, nsim)

  out <- data.frame(parity = numeric(nsim), payback = numeric(nsim), nb40 = numeric(nsim))
  for (i in seq_len(nsim)) {
    p <- list(C_inv = d$C_inv[i], C_nat = d$C_nat[i], K_inv = d$K_inv[i],
              r_inv = d$r_inv[i], r_nat = d$r_nat[i])
    p$D <- debt(d$AGB_inv[i], d$f_rel[i], d$dSOC[i], d$E_op[i])
    out$parity[i]  <- parity_time(p)
    out$payback[i] <- payback_time(p)
    out$nb40[i]    <- net_benefit(CREDIT, p)
  }
  out
}

sims <- lapply(SYS, simulate_system)
names(sims) <- SYS

# summarise: median and 95 percent interval of parity time among draws that reach parity,
# and the probability that parity is never reached inside the 300 year horizon
res_mc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(SYS, function(sid) {
  s  <- sims[[sid]]
  ok <- is.finite(s$parity)
  q  <- if (any(ok)) quantile(s$parity[ok], c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)) else rep(NA_real_, 3)
  data.frame(system_id = sid,
             p_never   = mean(!ok),
             parity_lo = q[1], parity_md = q[2], parity_hi = q[3],
             nb40_md   = median(s$nb40),
             nb40_lo   = quantile(s$nb40, 0.025),
             nb40_hi   = quantile(s$nb40, 0.975),
             p_nb40_neg = mean(s$nb40 < 0),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
rownames(res_mc) <- NULL

res <- merge(merge(sysmeta, res_point, by = "system_id"), res_mc, by = "system_id")
res <- res[order(res$display_order), ]
```

```{r}
#| label: crediting-test
#| echo: true

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The crediting test
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two questions decide whether a removal project could be credited at all under the
# accounting rules the standards actually use.
#
# 1. Does the project generate a positive net benefit inside the crediting period? If
#    the removal trajectory is still below the counterfactual at year 40, there is
#    nothing to credit no matter how the rules are written.
# 2. Is the removal debt small enough to be waved through as de minimis? Verra permits
#    an omitted decrease in carbon stocks only where it is below 5 percent of the total
#    greenhouse gas benefit the project generates. A removal whose debt exceeds that
#    share of its own benefit must account for the debt explicitly, and no approved
#    methodology outside the matched baseline design provides a way to do so.

res$claimable   <- res$nb40_md > 0
res$debt_share  <- ifelse(res$nb40_md > 0, res$debt / res$nb40_md, NA_real_)
res$deminimis   <- is.finite(res$debt_share) & res$debt_share < DEMINIMIS
res$verdict <- ifelse(!res$claimable, "no claimable benefit at 40 yr",
               ifelse(res$deminimis,  "claimable, debt de minimis",
                                      "claimable, debt must be accounted"))

# headline values, defined here because the abstract quotes them and inline R is evaluated
# in document order
maxdebt   <- res$system_short[which.max(res$debt)]
maxdebt_v <- max(res$debt)
mindebt_v <- min(res$debt)
```

#| echo: true

aud <- read.csv(file.path(IN, "standards-audit.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
CRIT <- c(introduce_prohibited   = "Introduction prohibited",
          removal_named_eligible = "Removal a named eligible activity",
          removal_creditable_carbon = "Carbon effect of removal creditable",
          biomass_debt_resolved  = "Invader biomass debt resolved",
          species_named          = "Any invasive taxon named",
          creditable_non_carbon  = "Removal creditable under a non carbon instrument")

audm <- reshape(aud[, c("standard_short", "criterion", "code")],
                idvar = "standard_short", timevar = "criterion", direction = "wide")
names(audm) <- sub("^code\\.", "", names(audm))
audm <- audm[, c("standard_short", names(CRIT))]
STORD <- c("Verra", "Plan Vivo", "Gold Standard", "ACR", "CAR", "Article 6.4", "ACCU")
audm <- audm[match(STORD, audm$standard_short), ]

# Abstract

Removing an invasive plant is one of the few restoration actions with an unambiguous biodiversity rationale and no reliable way to pay for it. Carbon finance fails it for a reason that is arithmetic rather than administrative: a woody invader is itself a carbon stock, so clearing it registers as an emission against a carbon-rich baseline and meets, on its face, every test for baseline gaming. Whether removal is nevertheless a carbon gain depends on a quantity that has not been estimated, the time for recovering native vegetation to overtake the trajectory the invader would have followed if left in place. We adapt the carbon parity framework developed for biofuel and bioenergy accounting to invasive plant removal and apply it to `r nrow(sysmeta)` invaded systems spanning woody nitrogen-fixing invaders, a thicket-forming shrub, an annual grass, a wetland graminoid, a woody wetland tree and a floating aquatic. Removal debts span `r f1(mindebt_v)` to `r f1(maxdebt_v)` Mg C per hectare and parity times run from immediate to never, ordered by the functional type of the invader. Only `r n_quant` systems can be parameterised entirely from measurement, which is itself a finding: the recovery rate that dominates the calculation is the quantity the literature measures least. We then audit six voluntary carbon standards and one compliance scheme against their own current requirement documents. All restrict the introduction of invasive species, none credits the carbon consequence of removing them, and the one design that dissolves the problem, the dynamic matched baseline, is confined to forest in a single country. The activity is monetised only as biochar feedstock and as a biodiversity credit, neither of which rewards the land carbon effect. The parity calculation, not the standards text, should decide where carbon finance is the right instrument, and for much of the invaded world it is not.

# 1. Introduction

Invasive alien species are among the recognised direct drivers of biodiversity loss, and the first global assessment devoted to them concluded that they are also among the most expensive, with costs that have risen steeply over recent decades [@ipbes2023invasive; @diagne2021high]. The international response has set targets for their control, but the financing to meet those targets has no obvious source. The Kunming-Montreal framework asks parties to reduce the introduction and establishment of invasive species and, separately, to restore a substantial share of degraded ecosystems, while relying on private finance to help pay for both [@cbd2022kunming].

Restoration finance has consolidated around carbon, and invasive removal fits that instrument badly. Almost every other restoration action adds something: trees, wetland, soil carbon, structural complexity. Removal takes something away, and in the case of a woody invader what it takes away is biomass carbon that a carbon accountant is obliged to count. A proponent who clears a dense stand of an invasive tree has, on the face of the ledger, done what the market is designed to prevent. The clearing is deliberate, it is carried out by the proponent, and it is motivated by carbon finance. Those three facts are the standard test for baseline gaming, and a genuine restoration project satisfies all of them.

The scientific question underneath the accounting question has been answered only in fragments. A substantial literature quantifies what invasion does to ecosystem carbon, beginning with the finding that invasion alters carbon and nitrogen pools systematically and often upward [@liao2008altered; @vila2011ecological; @peltzer2010effects], and continuing into mechanism through soil biota, microbial biomass and heterotrophic respiration [@raheem2024unraveling; @he2025plant; @negesse2025plant]. A much thinner literature follows what happens after removal, and it is dominated by endpoints other than carbon. The most recent global synthesis of post-removal revegetation reports native cover recovering by nearly half and non-native cover falling by more than a quarter, with carbon appearing only as an ordering claim, that abundance recovers faster than carbon stocks, which recover faster than diversity [@ahmad2026turning]. The two halves have never been joined into the quantity a financing decision requires, which is the time the removal trajectory takes to overtake the counterfactual.

That quantity has a well developed analogue. Biofuel accounting confronted the same structure when it became clear that clearing native vegetation for an energy crop incurs an immediate carbon debt that the crop's annual savings must repay, with payback periods running to centuries in the worst cases [@fargione2008land; @searchinger2008use]. Forest bioenergy accounting then sharpened the idea by separating payback, the return to the pre-intervention stock, from parity, the point at which the intervention overtakes the trajectory the stand would otherwise have followed [@mitchell2012carbon]. Parity, not payback, is the quantity relevant to a counterfactual-based crediting system, and it is the quantity computed here. The same literature is candid about the framework's fragility, since methodological choices alone can move parity estimates by two orders of magnitude [@jonker2014carbon], which is why the accounting boundary and the counterfactual are fixed here before any result is computed.

The nearest existing treatment of invasive control as climate action concerns invasive mammals on islands [@honzak2024toward], where the eradication target holds no standing biomass and the accounting problem examined here never arises. That asymmetry between animal and woody-plant invaders is the gap this paper occupies.

Three questions follow. First, across invaded systems that differ in the functional type of the invader, how long is the time to carbon parity after removal, and in which systems is it never reached? Second, given those answers, could a removal project be credited under the accounting rules that carbon standards actually apply? Third, where the carbon answer is unfavourable, what instrument is appropriate instead?

# 2. Methods

## 2.1 Systems and the evidence base

```{r}
#| label: tbl-systems
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The seven invaded systems, the functional type of the invader, and the strength of the evidence available for each. Evidence class is assigned from the tiers of the parameters the system contributes: quantified systems carry a measured or derived value for every parameter that the parity calculation is sensitive to, indicative systems rely on at least one parameter transferred from elsewhere."

t1 <- sysmeta[order(sysmeta$display_order),
              c("system_short", "invader", "region", "functional_type", "evidence_class")]
names(t1) <- c("System", "Invader", "Region", "Functional type", "Evidence")
kable(t1, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(t1, file.path(TBL, "table-1-systems.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

Systems were selected to span the functional types across which the carbon consequence of removal is expected to differ, rather than to be a representative sample of invaded ecosystems, which the available data would not support. The selection is deliberately adversarial to the framing advanced here: it includes the systems in which removal is most likely to be a carbon loss as well as those in which it is most likely to be a gain.

The evidence classification in Table 1 is derived from the parameter tiers rather than asserted, so a system counts as quantified only where both ecosystem stocks and the invader's own aboveground carbon come from measurement or from arithmetic on measurements. On that test `r n_quant` of the `r nrow(sysmeta)` systems are quantified and `r n_indic` are indicative. That ratio is itself a result. It is not possible at present to assemble a fully measured parity calculation for most of the world's best known plant invasions, and the reader should treat the indicative systems as showing the sign and rough magnitude of an effect rather than its value.

## 2.2 The parity model

The model compares two futures from the moment of intervention. Under the leave scenario the invader is retained and total ecosystem carbon relaxes toward the asymptote of the invaded state. Under the remove scenario the stock falls instantaneously by the removal debt, then relaxes toward the native reference stock at the rate at which native vegetation reaccumulates carbon on cleared ground. Both trajectories take the monomolecular form, which is the standard representation of stock recovery toward a carrying capacity and requires only a starting stock, an asymptote and a rate constant.

The removal debt has three components: the fraction of the invader's own aboveground carbon released to the atmosphere within a year of clearing, any soil organic carbon lost to the disturbance itself, and the operational emissions of the clearing work. Carbon that leaves the site in durable form, as timber or biochar, is not part of the debt, which is why the biochar route discussed below changes the arithmetic rather than merely the finance.

Carbon parity is the first time at which the removal trajectory crosses the leave trajectory. Payback, reported alongside it, is the first time at which the removal trajectory returns to the pre-removal stock. The two differ whenever the invaded state is not at equilibrium, and the difference matters because a crediting system pays for the former while intuition tends to reach for the latter.

## 2.3 Parameterisation and uncertainty

```{r}
#| label: tbl-parameters
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Parameter values, dispersion and provenance. Tier A is measured in the cited source for that system with a dispersion estimate, B measured as a point estimate, C derived by arithmetic shown in this document, D transferred from another system or a global default. Every tier D parameter is a stated limitation."

t2 <- par_long[, c("system_id", "parameter", "value", "sd", "n", "units", "source_key", "tier")]
t2 <- t2[order(match(t2$system_id, sysmeta$system_id[order(sysmeta$display_order)]),
               match(t2$parameter, PARNAMES)), ]
names(t2) <- c("System", "Parameter", "Value", "SD", "n", "Units", "Source", "Tier")
kable(t2, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)
write.csv(t2, file.path(TBL, "table-2-parameters.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tier-summary
#| echo: true

tier_tab <- table(factor(par_long$tier, levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D")))
n_tierD  <- as.integer(tier_tab["D"])
n_par    <- nrow(par_long)
```

Of the `r n_par` parameters entering the model, `r as.integer(tier_tab["A"])` are measured with a reported dispersion, `r as.integer(tier_tab["B"])` are measured point estimates, `r as.integer(tier_tab["C"])` are derived by arithmetic set out in the code above, and `r n_tierD` are transferred from another system or taken as a global default. The last group is concentrated in the recovery rate, which is the least measured and most influential parameter in the model, a point we return to.

Uncertainty is propagated by Monte Carlo with `r f0(NSIM)` draws per system. Each parameter is drawn from a normal distribution centred on its point estimate, truncated where the physical meaning requires it, with the dispersion its source reports. Where a source reports none, the parameter is assigned a coefficient of variation of `r f2(DEFAULT_CV)`, and the sensitivity of the conclusions to that assumption is examined directly.

## 2.4 Standards audit

Six crediting regimes were audited against their own current requirement documents rather than against summaries: the Verra Verified Carbon Standard together with the Climate, Community and Biodiversity Standards, Plan Vivo, the Gold Standard, the American Carbon Registry, the Climate Action Reserve, and the Article 6.4 mechanism of the Paris Agreement. The Australian Carbon Credit Unit scheme was added as the one compliance regime in which suppression of non-native plants appears in statute. Each document was retrieved, its full text searched for the relevant terms, and each occurrence read in context, because the phrase appears in a great many project documents as a compliance negation, a statement that invasive species will not be introduced, which is the opposite of the activity at issue.

# 3. Results

## 3.1 Time to carbon parity

```{r}
#| label: parity-values
#| echo: true

# values quoted in this section, computed rather than typed
res_ok    <- res[is.finite(res$parity_md), ]
res_never <- res[res$p_never > 0.5, ]
fastest   <- res_ok$system_short[which.min(res_ok$parity_md)]
fastest_t <- min(res_ok$parity_md, na.rm = TRUE)
slowest   <- res_ok$system_short[which.max(res_ok$parity_md)]
slowest_t <- max(res_ok$parity_md, na.rm = TRUE)
n_neg40   <- sum(res$nb40_md < 0)
```

Removal debts span `r f1(mindebt_v)` to `r f1(maxdebt_v)` Mg C per hectare, a range of more than an order of magnitude, and they order the systems almost exactly as the functional type of the invader would predict. The largest debt falls on `r maxdebt`, where the invader is itself the dominant carbon pool of the system, and the smallest on systems where the invader holds negligible standing biomass and its effect on carbon runs through suppression of the native community rather than through its own stock.

Parity times follow from that ordering but not proportionally, because repayment depends on the gap between the native asymptote and the invaded stock rather than on the debt alone. Among systems that reach parity at all, the range runs from `r yr(fastest_t)` years in `r fastest` to `r yr(slowest_t)` years in `r slowest`. `r nrow(res_never)` of the `r nrow(res)` systems do not reach parity within the three-century horizon in the majority of Monte Carlo draws, and `r n_neg40` are still below the counterfactual at the end of a forty year crediting period.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-parity
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Removal debt, time to carbon parity and time to carbon payback, with the net carbon benefit of removal at the end of a 40 year crediting period. Parity times are medians with 95 percent intervals taken over the Monte Carlo draws that reach parity, so they are conditional on parity being reached and must be read alongside the adjacent probability that it is not. Systems in which the majority of draws never reach parity are reported as not reached rather than by a conditional median. Payback is the point estimate. Negative net benefit means the removal trajectory is still below the counterfactual at year 40."

t3 <- data.frame(
  System    = res$system_short,
  `Debt (Mg C/ha)` = f1(res$debt),
  `Parity (yr)` = ifelse(res$p_never > 0.5, "not reached",
                    paste0(yr(res$parity_md), " (", yr(res$parity_lo), "-", yr(res$parity_hi), ")")),
  `P(never)` = pc(res$p_never),
  `Payback (yr)` = yr(res$payback),
  `Net benefit at 40 yr (Mg C/ha)` = paste0(f1(res$nb40_md), " (", f1(res$nb40_lo), " to ", f1(res$nb40_hi), ")"),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(t3, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(t3, file.path(TBL, "table-3-parity.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

Parity is the crossing, payback the return to the pre-removal stock, and the shaded area the cumulative carbon cost carried until parity. Right, the three outcomes the framework distinguishes, drawn from the fitted systems."

png(file.path(FIG, "figure-1-concept.png"), width = 2700, height = 1260, res = 300)

# payback and parity marked at different heights so the labels cannot collide
segments(Tb, ylim_a[1], Tb, ps$C_inv, lty = 3, col = "grey45")

## 3.2 Sensitivity

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity
#| echo: true

# One at a time elasticity: the proportional change in parity time produced by a ten
# percent increase in each parameter, holding the rest at their point estimates. Where
# parity is not reached at either the base or the perturbed value the elasticity is
# undefined and reported as such.
#
# One subtlety has to be handled explicitly. Where a source gives no invaded asymptote the
# assembly step sets K_inv equal to C_inv, so the retention trajectory is flat. Perturbing
# C_inv alone would then leave a stale K_inv below the new starting stock and the retention
# curve would bend downward, which is an artefact of the perturbation rather than a property
# of the system. K_inv is therefore moved with C_inv wherever the two were tied.
static_invaded <- sapply(SYS, function(s) isTRUE(all.equal(pars_point[[s]]$K_inv,
                                                           pars_point[[s]]$C_inv)))
names(static_invaded) <- SYS

elasticity <- function(sid, p_name, delta = 0.10) {
  p0 <- pars_point[[sid]]
  t0 <- parity_time(p0)
  p1 <- p0
  p1[[p_name]] <- p0[[p_name]] * (1 + delta)
  if (p_name == "C_inv" && static_invaded[[sid]]) p1$K_inv <- p1$C_inv
  p1$D <- debt(p1$AGB_inv, p1$f_rel, p1$dSOC, p1$E_op)
  t1 <- parity_time(p1)
  if (!is.finite(t0) || !is.finite(t1) || t0 == 0) return(NA_real_)
  ((t1 - t0) / t0) / delta
}

ELP <- c("C_nat", "r_nat", "AGB_inv", "f_rel", "dSOC", "C_inv")
# short axis labels; the full parameter definitions are in Table 2
ELLAB <- c(C_nat = "Native stock", r_nat = "Recovery rate", AGB_inv = "Invader AGB",
           f_rel = "Released fraction", dSOC = "Soil C loss", C_inv = "Invaded stock")
elas <- outer(SYS, ELP, Vectorize(function(s, p) elasticity(s, p)))
dimnames(elas) <- list(sysmeta$system_short[match(SYS, sysmeta$system_id)], ELP)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensitivity
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Elasticity of the time to carbon parity to a ten per cent increase in each parameter, by system. A value of minus one means a ten per cent increase in the parameter shortens the parity time by ten per cent. Green shortens parity, red lengthens it. The colour scale is clipped at the ninetieth percentile of absolute elasticity so that a single large value cannot flatten the rest of the panel; the printed values are unclipped. Rows marked undefined are systems in which parity is not reached, where a proportional change in the parity time has no meaning."

png(file.path(FIG, "figure-3-sensitivity.png"), width = 2400, height = 1250, res = 300)
op <- par(mar = c(3.0, 10.5, 1.6, 1.0), family = "sans")
z <- t(elas)                                   # parameters on x, systems on y
# the colour scale is clipped at the 90th percentile of absolute elasticity so that a single
# large value cannot flatten the rest of the panel; printed values are unclipped
zcap <- quantile(abs(z), 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
zc   <- pmin(pmax(z, -zcap), zcap)
brk  <- seq(-zcap, zcap, length.out = 21)
pal  <- colorRampPalette(c("#2f6b4f", "#f2f2ee", "#9b3b3b"))(20)
image(seq_len(nrow(zc)), seq_len(ncol(zc)), zc, col = pal, breaks = brk,
      axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
for (i in seq_len(nrow(z)))
  mtext(unname(ELLAB[rownames(z)[i]]), side = 1, at = i, line = 0.5, cex = 0.66, las = 1)
for (j in seq_len(ncol(z)))
  mtext(colnames(z)[j], side = 2, at = j, line = 0.4, cex = 0.7, las = 1, adj = 1)
abline(h = seq_len(ncol(z)) + 0.5, col = "white", lwd = 3)
abline(v = seq_len(nrow(z)) + 0.5, col = "white", lwd = 3)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(z))) for (j in seq_len(ncol(z)))
  if (is.finite(z[i, j])) text(i, j, sprintf("%.1f", z[i, j]), cex = 0.66, col = "grey15")
# systems where parity is never reached carry no elasticity at all: say so on the panel
for (j in seq_len(ncol(z))) if (all(!is.finite(z[, j])))
  text(mean(seq_len(nrow(z))), j, "parity not reached, elasticity undefined",
       cex = 0.66, col = "grey45", font = 3)
par(op); invisible(dev.off())
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG, "figure-3-sensitivity.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity-values
#| echo: true

mean_abs <- sort(colMeans(abs(elas), na.rm = TRUE), decreasing = TRUE)
top_par  <- names(mean_abs)[1]
top_val  <- unname(mean_abs[1])
second   <- names(mean_abs)[2]
second_v <- unname(mean_abs[2])

# effect of the assumed dispersion on unreported parameters: rerun the ordering with a
# coefficient of variation of 0.10 and 0.40 and check that the ranking of systems holds
rank_base <- rank(ifelse(is.finite(res$parity_md), res$parity_md, Inf))
```

The parity time is most sensitive to `r top_par`, with a mean absolute elasticity of `r f2(top_val)` across systems, and second most sensitive to `r second` at `r f2(second_v)`. An elasticity of one means that a ten per cent change in the parameter moves the parity time by ten per cent. Elasticities on the recovery rate are negative throughout, as they must be, since faster native reaccumulation shortens the time to parity. Elasticities on the invader's own aboveground stock and on the released fraction are positive, since both enlarge the debt.

The practical consequence is uncomfortable. The parameter that matters most is the one the literature measures least. Standing stocks in invaded and uninvaded states are widely reported, frequently with dispersion and sample sizes, whereas the rate at which native vegetation reaccumulates carbon after clearance is reported almost nowhere, and where it is reported it comes from a chronosequence rather than a time series.

## 3.3 The crediting gap

```{r}
#| label: tbl-audit
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Audit of six voluntary carbon standards and one compliance scheme against their own current requirement documents. 0 absent, 1 permitted or implied, 2 explicit. Documents, clauses and retrieval dates are given in the input table."

t4 <- audm
names(t4) <- c("Standard", unname(CRIT))
kable(t4, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(t4, file.path(TBL, "table-4-standards.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```
